title: Democrats Spend $163 Million Making Trump the Face of the Midterms
excerpt: Democratic ads mentioning the president have aired nearly 180,000 times since September 1, while Republicans have spent just $11 million on ads naming their own leader, an AP analysis found.
body:
• Democratic candidates and allies have spent more than $163 million since September 1 on TV advertising that mentions President Trump, airing nearly 180,000 times, an Associated Press analysis of AdImpact data found.
  • Republicans have spent just $11 million on ads mentioning their own party's president — about 16,000 airings — a conspicuous silence about the GOP's dominant but unpopular leader.
  • The Democratic ads tie Republican candidates to Trump on tariffs, the Iran war and health premiums; Trump's own instruction to voters is to pretend he is on the ballot.
  • Control of Congress decided on November 3 sets the terrain for immigration enforcement and visa policy fights that directly affect Indian American families.

President Donald Trump says he wants voters to pretend he is on the ballot in this year's midterm elections. By the evidence of the advertising market, Democrats agree with him — and are paying far more than Republicans to make the election a referendum on a president who is not actually running.

A lopsided air war

Democratic candidates and their allies have spent more than $163 million since September 1 on television advertising mentioning Trump, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks media spending. Ads referencing the president ran nearly 180,000 times across broadcast, cable and streaming. Republican ads mentioning Trump ran about 16,000 times at an estimated $11 million — a noticeable quiet around the party's dominant yet unpopular leader.

The Democratic template is consistent: bind the Republican candidate to Trump, then to prices. In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff's campaign has spent nearly $3 million on an ad attacking Rep. Mike Collins for voting for Trump's tariffs and the Iran war and to double health insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians. Tariffs and war-driven costs are the through-line — issues where Democrats believe the president is a liability even with voters who backed him.

The Republican counter

Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre argued the spending reflected Democratic hollowness rather than strength: "Democrats are lighting money on fire talking about President Trump because they have no agenda other than investigation, obstruction and impeachment," she said, in remarks carried by the AP. Meanwhile Trump is rallying in Georgia despite visible party divisions there — one state Republican, Perry, told the AP, "I don't speak for him, and he doesn't speak for me."

Why it matters beyond the ads

Midterm ad strategy is really a bet on turnout: Democrats are wagering that anti-Trump motivation outperforms economic messaging in a low-turnout election, while Republicans are wagering their voters will show up without the president's name in the creative. For Indian American voters — a constituency both parties courted hard in 2024 — the outcome decides who holds committee gavels over immigration enforcement, visa processing and the H-1B programme in 2027. The spending gap closes on November 3; the policy consequences run for two years.
